name: Magnesium oil / Epsom salt bath

card.summary: Soaking in magnesium sulfate or applying magnesium chloride brine, popular for transdermal magnesium claims that have little published trial support.
card.aka: Epsom salt bath, magnesium flakes, transdermal magnesium
card.note: Sources reviewed contain no trials of skin absorption or appearance effects.

quick.overview:
Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, long sold as bath salts for sore muscles and feet. Magnesium oil is a concentrated magnesium chloride brine applied to skin. Online, both are promoted as ways to raise magnesium levels through the skin, for sleep, recovery and relaxation.

The sources reviewed for this entry do not include trials of absorption through skin or of any appearance outcome.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that magnesium passes through the skin during a soak or topical application. Encyclopedic sources describe bath use for soothing sore feet and its role in bath salts, without stating that skin absorption occurs.
quick.risks: Magnesium sulfate is given internally in medicine for deficiency and other conditions, where dosing is clinical. Epsom salt in baths is widely sold over the counter; no safety data from the sources reviewed address bath use specifically.

lead: Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate heptahydrate) baths and magnesium oil (a concentrated magnesium chloride brine sprayed on skin) are used for transdermal magnesium, with the aim of better sleep, muscle recovery, relaxation and smoother-feeling skin, and in some hair-loss circles for the scalp. People use them as a wind-down and recovery routine that supports training and rest, and so indirectly their physique and appearance.[1][2]

Epsom salt is named after a saline spring in Epsom, Surrey, England, and is used externally as bath salts, especially foot soaks for sore feet.[1] Magnesium oil is not an oil; Wikipedia notes the hexahydrate form of magnesium chloride is sometimes advertised under that name.[3]

Whether magnesium crosses the skin in meaningful amounts is the central research question. A 2017 review in Nutrients concluded that claims for transdermal magnesium are not scientifically supported, while calling for larger and longer human studies.[2]

paras: Magnesium sulfate takes its common name from a bitter spring at Epsom, Surrey, where it was obtained from water emerging where chalk meets clay. [1] It was historically also used to treat lead poisoning and widely by veterinarians in the early-to-mid twentieth century. [1]

A 2017 literature review by Gröber and colleagues reports that the stratum corneum is a water-repellent barrier that hydrated magnesium ions cross poorly, and that hair follicles and sweat glands may allow some passage but cover only about 0.1% to 1% of the skin.[2]

The review describes a University of Birmingham study of 19 people taking daily 12-minute Epsom salt baths for a week, in which most had higher blood magnesium, though often by small amounts and with results published only on an industry-linked website. A study of spa-water immersion found no change in plasma magnesium after two hours. A 12-week study of nine people using magnesium oil spray and foot soaks reported an average 59.7% rise in hair magnesium, which the authors note is a weak indicator of body magnesium and was a tiny sample.[2]

A 2017 pilot study of 25 randomised participants using magnesium cream (56 mg per day) for two weeks found a small serum rise that was not statistically significant overall, with significance only in a non-athlete subgroup.[2]

Internally, magnesium sulfate serves as replacement therapy for magnesium deficiency and in hospital for abnormal magnesium levels and constipation, with other uses including arrhythmias, eclampsia seizure prevention and asthma. [1] These uses involve clinical administration rather than bathing.

The 2017 review notes a phase I trial of a magnesium-containing skin protectant lotion in 34 volunteers, applied three times daily for three days, which reported no serious adverse effects or toxic magnesium levels; it was designed as a protectant rather than a supplement.[2] Wikipedia notes magnesium toxicity from oral magnesium chloride is rare in healthy people because kidneys excrete excess, and that large oral amounts can cause diarrhoea.[3]

A looksmax.org thread asks about magnesium oil for hair growth or hair loss. The post says magnesium oil has been used by many against hair loss, that no objective studies measured its effect on hair growth, and proposes that magnesium could reduce scalp calcification linked to DHT-driven TGF-beta activity in androgenetic alopecia.[4]

No studies found on appearance outcomes of Epsom salt baths or magnesium oil. Human studies on transdermal magnesium absorption are small: the Birmingham bath study (19 people), a magnesium-oil study of nine people, and a two-week magnesium cream pilot (25 randomised),[2] and a laboratory study used magnesium oil in a methotrexate nanogel for arthritis in animals.[5]

lore.intro: Magnesium oil and Epsom baths are discussed in wellness and hair-loss circles as ways to deliver magnesium through the skin.[4]

claims.claim: Magnesium absorbs through the skin and raises body magnesium.
claims.believers: Proponents cite the Birmingham bath data and the magnesium oil study showing a higher hair magnesium level.[2]
claims.experts: The 2017 review concluded the claims are not scientifically supported and called for larger, longer human studies.[2]

claims.claim: Magnesium oil helps hair loss by reducing scalp calcification.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org post proposes magnesium could reduce DHT-linked scalp calcification and so hair loss.[4]
claims.experts: The same post notes no objective studies have measured magnesium oil's effect on hair growth.[4]

angle.text: Users take Epsom salt baths or spray magnesium oil to relax, sleep and recover from training, and some apply it to the scalp or skin for hair and complexion. The route from soak to looks is indirect, through sleep, recovery and relaxation.
